classIntro.text: So it's a rare full class. I can't — I don't think it's ever happened. I feel bad for whoever I'm missing.

classIntro.speaker: Kadam Kyle
classIntro.text:
It's something. Maybe that was the key. Yeah, exactly. Okay, well that's very lovely, so it's very nice for us all to be back together, and we'll have a nice time getting back in the text. We're starting on getting into rejoicing today, and I'm just going to say a little bit about it right now because we're about to engage in the practice. And there's something related to it that's very helpful, and we'll do a meditation on this.

So as it says in the text very soon, rejoicing is a practice you can do while lying down. Lying down — the implication is it's a very powerful practice that's also completely restful. And it's completely relaxed. And it's incredibly pure, because you can't have an ulterior motive for rejoicing. There's no outer activity. It's just an inner activity that's just completely pure, and it's focused on virtue. So it's a very, very powerful practice, and we're going to learn more about it. But this interesting quality is that it's such a restful practice. It's famously something you can do while lying down — just laying there on the couch, but rejoicing incredibly.

Anyway, the point is it's this attitude of restfulness that's very, very nice to connect to. And in reality, all Dharma practice is restful. It's only our grasping that makes things more than that. It's just our grasping that results at a self, something we're attached to — that's the only thing that makes things not restful. All Dharma practice is restful because things are like a dream. There's no need to fret in a dream. They don't need to be intense in a dream.

So while we do the practice right now, you can just see — what's it like to just do it in a far more restful way than normal? And then just put down any striving, or whatever that New York energy that you might have caught 40 years ago is — just put it down. And see, can I just do this in a completely restful way, this practice? We're gentle, very comfortable. And if you come up with something, just see — could I do it even more restful than that? You might realize, oh yeah, there's another layer under that one. Oh, that's even nicer. Like that.

Anyway, that's all I wanted to say, just because it might be useful as we go into this meditation. And then at the end of the prayers, we'll do a meditation on rejoicing itself. We'll just maybe rejoice in our Sangha friends, for example, which is a very nice thing to kick off our class with. Okay, so let's enjoy. Thank you.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy, May everyone be free from misery, May no one ever be separated from their happiness, May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate, and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the Wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind Teacher, source of all good; O Bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O Bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just as the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara's pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O Bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma's root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara's ocean; O So that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva's ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the common path, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy Teachers, O Bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect Teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
First we can completely relax. We can let any tension in our body and mind melt away. The object of our meditation is the mind of rejoicing. Rejoicing is a mind free of any jealousy, pride, or other delusions that delights in the virtue we see. By rejoicing we start to adopt the virtue that we are appreciating and create abundant merit to gain that trait. We also overcome jealousy, which is a completely purposeless delusion.

We can then go one by one through our TTP Sangha friends and just rejoice in some virtue that you see in them. It could be any of the obvious virtues — their wisdom, compassion, contentment, patience. Or it could just be their persistence in the face of certain challenges, or their effort in trying to deal with their delusions.

As you celebrate their virtues in your Sangha friends, the feeling of rejoicing arises in your heart. And the admiring and wishing for that quality yourself — can just hold that single-pointedly for as long as possible.

And then in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Okay, we'll begin by reading the root text.

shantidevaReading.text:
Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life. It's an easy one, four verses, page 29, 1–4.

(1) With great gladness I rejoice
In the virtues that protect living beings
From the sufferings of the lower realms
And lead all those who suffer to fortunate realms.

(2) I rejoice in the accumulation of virtue
That releases living beings from samsaric rebirth
And leads them to the state of nirvana —
The supreme, permanent inner peace.

(3) I rejoice in the enlightenment of the Conqueror Buddhas
And in the spiritual paths of the Bodhisattvas.

(4) With delight I rejoice in the ocean of virtue
That arises from generating the mind of enlightenment, bodhichitta,
Which brings happiness to all living beings,
And in the deeds that benefit those beings.

Okay, very good. A rare two-line verse — what's going on there? No idea. Okay, lovely.

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text: So in a moment we'll be sharing some data. I'll remind us all of the injunction with respect to sharing data. Maybe someone could remind us, so I don't have to say it. What's the three-point structure? This isn't to be rulesy, right? It's actually to cherish the rest of our class so people can get a chance to say something if they want to. And it's actually helpful for us to speak with a discipline — not just stream of consciousness, given them the whole Lord of the Rings every time we speak or something like that. War and Peace, whatever. Yeah, so what are the three points?

postReading.speaker: David
postReading.text: There's a three-point structure. So, one: here's what happened — a brief synopsis of the situation that you were in, or the scenario in which you practiced, like what was going on. Number two: here's what I practiced in that situation. Then three: here's how it went or didn't go. And then what lessons can I draw from that?

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text: Yeah, that's it. That's exactly right. Thank you.

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text:
But if you do not abide by the structure, I'll note in my mind, and then you're going to be given a special task in the future — to write down what you say before you say it. So if you want to say it, you have to have it written down. So this is very helpful. It's a good exercise anyway, actually, because you start to see — oh, what's all the garbledygook coming out of my mind? This is actually the point.

And we're going to be doing more group discussions in TTP, and this will be the demand — that any question that you want to ask has to be written down first. And you'll see, it makes everything so much better when a question's written down. Like, I was just in ITTP and we have group discussion every four classes. I found this such a helpful exercise. Every class, we'd have a group discussion. I would come with my questions prepared, and some of the questions would be on a piece of paper with eight iterations of the question. Like, this was the first try. No, cross out that word. Cross out that point. Okay, this is the second try. Ah, no, that's not even close. Okay, let's get to the third one. Like that. And eventually getting to something that was really helpful and practical for myself and others. It's like editing, right?

So anyway, I'm not trying to say this to scare us. I'm just encouraging us to have some discipline so that we can all share and hear from each other and learn from each other. And I hope that's okay. Okay, good. Thank you. So I'm excited to send my first note when it gets a chance. We won't announce it. We won't put it on the wall. Okay. Anyone like to share any data from the last six weeks?

practiceReports.speaker: Anne K
practiceReports.text: So, my main practice all summer was really to take this bodhichitta thing seriously. And how could I do that? So it has to be all living beings. So I tried to keep the six realms in mind all the time. Like, I'm never going to abandon all beings of the six realms. And my practice was to talk to them out loud when I was getting ready for work — I haven't abandoned you, I am here for you, I'm on your side, I'm doing everything I can today to help you. And then all throughout the day I would try to keep them in mind and try to share whatever good feelings I had or good experiences I had with them consciously. Whether it was like peace in my heart, or getting praise, or delicious — I didn't eat many sandwiches, sometimes salad, sometimes cake. Oh, see, I've gone too far. I'm getting into Lord of the Rings.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, you're in book two now. No, no, no. You're still on target. Yeah, okay. I love it. So you practiced thinking of the six realms all day.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne K
practiceReports.text: Yeah, and it felt wonderful. And everything I enjoyed, I enjoyed so much more — sharing it with everybody. And I felt so whole and complete and happy. Where I wasn't able to do it was when I got so busy and overscheduled that I simply was not able to include that. And so, order of operations, I had to constantly pare back my schedule so I could get back to the place where I could keep that in mind and remain mindful of that. And I'm going to continue that going forward because it was terrific.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, it's fantastic, Anne. It's Nagarjuna's advice that every day we think about the beings in the lower realms. Geshe-la explains it in some book somewhere, and all six realms is kind of implied. Yeah, thank you. And it's such a simple practice, but just that awareness starts to really give us all the Lamrim objects quite naturally. Versus if we just think about ourselves in this world, we're just earthbound people — we're actually like an animal mind, just living, scurrying through our day, getting things done, surviving, procreating, making friends, sleeping, eating. So just thinking about the six realms, we become a spiritual being. And then everything else that followed was really nice. And you noticed busyness was the sort of tension there, and the more you value the six realm practice, the more you're able to pare back the busyness of it. Thank you, lovely, so much. Thank you. Next person.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text:
So mine are post-festival, trying to hold on to how I came home. One is in seated practice, to reduce distractions — I saw a snippet of one of the Kadampa podcast conversations where a nun said that she practices: she meditates on death briefly before she meditates, all of her meditations. And this is what hit home with me, and I've been doing it — what if this is the last time I'm doing this meditation? And it's just made my concentration so much stronger. And if I get distracted, I just come back to: this is the last time you can do this meditation. Do it for good, do it for real.

And my break practice has been imputing Vajrayogini and Heruka on everybody I see. So that if they're pure, I'm obviously in a pure land — if I'm seeing them purely, they're pure. I really try to do it with people who I find maybe annoying. I try to do it overall, just to purify. I'm just purifying Brooklyn so that all those Vajrayoginis and Herukas can see our new building. But in day-to-day life, it really has made a difference in just relaxing me and just making nothing else matter, because it's all mere name. So it's a lot of bringing emptiness into it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Thanks, Fran. Yeah, lovely. Glad that you could bring some of what you got from the festival back into daily life, and especially that practice of trying to see people as Buddhas, or in the best way possible. Yeah, lovely.

practiceReports.speaker: Adriana
practiceReports.text:
Okay, so the focus of my summer has been on accepting defeat and offering the victory. And I've had a lot of opportunities to practice — in moving, in my apartment, the selling of my apartment, and then at my work now everything is getting restructured. And so people are kind of like vying to hold on to their little piece of job, and so I've noticed that people are crueler.

Yeah, so the good thing is that I had a lot of opportunities to practice. Where people insulted me, and then what I found that worked is I took a little pause where I just said: oh, is this correct? Do I agree? And then sometimes I'd be like, I'm not sure. Or sometimes like, maybe they're right. Or no, they're wrong. But just the little — it's like a millisecond of just like an objective evaluation of it — so it didn't feel personal in the moment. And I'm not exaggerating when I say like, I can't wait for it to happen again. It's so cool to be okay with people putting you down, because it has nothing to do with you. So it was really fun. Thanks.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Thanks, Adriana. Yeah, so practicing with criticism, especially accepting defeat and offering the victory. And you used a little practice which is: step one, pause. Step two, ask — is it true or not? And then basically go from there. Yeah, which is a classic Dharma criticism practice, right?

Is it true or not? And then if it is, great — they're just helping us see something we don't see, or showing us that everyone else sees it even though we think it's hidden. And then if it's not true, it has nothing to do with us. It's just their own stuff. So there's no reason to be bothered. So in both cases, it's a win-win. It's easier said than done, right? Our little survival instinct doesn't like it. But yeah, exactly. But it is very meaningful. Glad that you could be practicing that this summer.

practiceReports.speaker: Mimi
practiceReports.text:
All right. So I taught the family Dharma class. And you know, just coming back from festival and going back to work, everything kind of just was really at a fast clip. And I had two new assistants coming to help me with the class. And I was like, oh gosh, I don't know who's going to come, right? Like if it's going to be well attended — it wasn't, nobody registered.

So I don't know, I was getting prepared. I was here early, I was getting prepared. I was in the lobby, in the little waiting room, and Ryan very quietly said to me: Mimi, so what are you doing? And I'm like, I'm going to teach the Dharma class, the children's class. And he said, well, what's your intention? And I was like, to help the children meet the Dharma. And I was like, to help them — free them from samsara. But in all joking aside, it really stopped me to make me think: what am I doing? What is the purpose? What is my intention?

Okay, so the class — the time came. There was nobody coming in. And I was a little bit concerned about my assistants — I wanted them to also experience having come and taken the time to actually see a class. Ten minutes in, nothing. So I was like, okay, well, so this is how the class goes. And right as I thought we weren't going to have anybody, in comes Susanna with her three children and the grandma. And they were just so happy, just so happy to be in the class.

So here's what happened. I taught, we did a little meditation — it's just a very simple breathing meditation — and all the three children, grandma, and Susanna were all lined up with my two assistants. And I just opened my eyes and I saw them just meditating and enjoying. And especially the little baby — she had closed her eyes, she was crisscross applesauce, sitting there. And my heart just — I just cried. I was crying. And I was so happy for them, and happy for Susanna. I was like, oh, what a beautiful job she's done with these children. So I think I practiced rejoicing.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Very good. Thank you very much. It's lovely. And yeah, maybe your practice of checking the intention also helped, thanks to your kind Sangha friend pressing your intention — that might have helped even make it even more pure and kind and loving. And hopefully that was beneficial to the people who came, and you were able to rejoice in their happiness. Thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: David
practiceReports.text:
So I think I also practiced a lot of rejoicing at the festival. And I think my takeaway this time around was the same as actually when I went to Brazil a couple years ago, which was just feeling extremely grateful for Geshe-la's kindness. And just seeing all the thought and preparation that went into the most efficient Dharma delivery mechanism — just like seeing the hundreds of people having the teachings translated into their languages. And yeah, just how beautiful the teachings were.

And again, like Gen-la Jampa's presentation also — I felt like just extremely beautifully highlighted Geshe-la's words, and he just really kind of elevated them in just an exquisitely beautiful way. And also having the opportunity to visit the meditation room where Geshe-la taught for decades — it was just such a holy place and just could really palpably feel the blessings just like pouring through that place.

And so yeah, and the time since I got back, really tried to focus on his words when we're doing the sort of the Lamrim practice and Mirror of Dharma and elevating those. And yeah, just trying to honor his vision. I remember one time when Gen-la Dekyong visited here, I asked her — I was like, you know, there's so many different practices, I can't tell what my biggest problem is, like where should I start. And she said, just — like you're in a study program, right? Why don't you just do that? And I was like, oh — she said it in a much, much more kind way, but that was sort of the gist of it. And I was like, oh yeah, that's a really good idea, Gen-la Dekyong. Thank you.

So yeah, so I'm just really, really grateful to be back here and excited to decide on our practice at the end of class and really just go for it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thanks, David. I'm really glad. Yeah, this is one of the benefits of the festival — it's just a rejoicing opportunity. Everywhere you look, there's just so many ways to rejoice and to celebrate, and that's very inspiring and powerful.

My version of what you were describing — it hadn't happened a bunch of times, but one was in what's called the Education Council meeting, which happens every summer festival, where the General Spiritual Director meets with all the resident teachers and they give a talk, some special words. And so Geshe-la started that tradition, and the next General Spiritual Director did that, and the next one. So Gen-la Dekyong did it for 16 years as the General Spiritual Director. And this is the first year Gen-la Dekyong did it.

And I was profoundly moved in that, in different ways. But actually, the sort of vision of succession really moved me. And I was thinking, this is so amazing — like, this is just a different person, this isn't the same person, but everything else is working just as beautifully and as blessed as always.

And the kind of architecture of an organization is an incredibly complicated thing to figure out, right? Some people are like anti-joiners — against organizations. What does that mean? Against families? Or against clubs? Like, what's your issue with an organization? Like you just want disorganization? Yeah, it actually takes courage to join an organization and to commit to something and try to make it better. Like, it's actually cowardice to be a non-joiner. It's just cowardice.

And so when people create an organization, it's not perfect. But there can be better ones or better designed ones or worse designed ones. And it's very complicated to create a very good organization, one that works and functions and has to deal with all the challenges that come from creating a structure. And one of the most challenging things in the spiritual tradition is succession, right? How do you pass the baton? Even in political organizations, this is very complicated. How do you do it? What's the best way? How do you make sure the right person gets chosen? How do you make sure it's not someone who just blows the whole thing up? How do you make sure that everything kind of moves forward skillfully and effectively? It's not an easy question. And many traditions are not able to do that. They just die very quickly — one generation in, or two generations in, or zero generations in, sorry.

And so I was just sitting there feeling very touched, thinking, wow, this is beautiful — the structure and the whole transmission sort of process. And that everything was just peaceful and easy and comfortable, and everyone was just inspired and happy, and doing their own thing and doing their practice and improving. And I thought, I wouldn't be able to have figured out the best way to do this, and it's working very smoothly. So anyway, I was just rejoicing also in that way.

Yeah, thanks, David. Kristin, and then Sumit.

practiceReports.speaker: Kristin
practiceReports.text:
So I have two things that I could report, but I put one in the chat, so I won't repeat it in the interest of time and letting other people have an opportunity also. But another more recent thing that I encountered — well, I studied for the exam, and to be honest, it was not as successful as I think my past exams, particularly with regard to memorization. And so I've been reflecting on that.

And I have a patient who worked as an actor, but he is an older person that has had a stroke — no speech difficulties, but many others. And he was telling me that he's memorizing a six-page monologue for this performance and hadn't done something like that in a while. And I was just really impressed. And he was reflecting on how the mind works and his ability to kind of recover the skill of memorization. And I was asking a bit about the process and how you do that. And he was just sharing — one thing that's helpful is to just sort of sleep with it, to just read a little section, repeat that section, and then as you're sort of falling asleep, you're sort of reciting it to yourself. And then you're gradually building on that. So you're kind of just like all day, every day, sort of trying to marinate in it.

And so I have a renewed commitment to trying to memorize Dharma. And I realized in the conversation that there are like four lines of Shakespeare that I memorized as a high schooler that I still know. And I feel like my memory is not what it was then. So I feel like I have also this fire of like, I've got to do this while there's time to store it in long-term storage. So that's my report.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thanks, Kristin. It's a nice way to approach working for an exam and not really feeling that it went how you want it to go — instead of being discouraged or negative about it, using it to see, okay, what went off here, and how can I refine it? And that's always just the right thing to do in any challenge. But that's a nice example. So you got a renewed commitment to improve your memorization practice. Now anyone who needs some tips around that, anytime, feel free to nudge me too, and I'm very happy to explain some methods that are extremely effective to memorize things. Very easy. Thank you so much. Yeah, Sumit.

practiceReports.speaker: Sumit
practiceReports.text:
So for me, the practice is going to Manjushri Center. And I think in a previous TTP discussion, you've been like, don't get into the details of things that happened — miraculous and stuff. So I want to honor that.

And what I guess I want to say is, one of the things — we come here and we're involved in this, and the tradition is: hey, be nice to people. And there's a certain logic and it all makes sense to us and we get that, and of course we learn those things and do those things. But it's not just that. This is religion. And in a religion, there are supernatural things. And to me, that's also part of our tradition.

And going to Manjushri Center made that more apparent to me. And I think that's very inspiring, very powerful. And just, I guess for me and maybe for others, this is a thing to lean into as well. There's a magic to this, to this tradition, to Buddhism. And so yeah, lean in and enjoy.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Thank you, Sumit. I wonder — just briefly, could you say, was there anything that you did from your own side to stimulate that sort of supernatural or magical quality that we could learn from or adopt ourselves? Because I get what you're saying, but I'm sure you did something to facilitate that, right?

practiceReports.speaker: Sumit
practiceReports.text:
I think one of the things is you have to have faith, right? I think that's — everybody knows that part. But I think when you know more, then it's like, you can see the connection between something. I'm trying to explain this very well.

Basically — okay, I'm getting too much detail. I learned about mandalas and the details, and so I meditate on that — that's part of my practice now. Something I know about — something will appear that, oh, that's like the mandala thing. I wouldn't have known that. You have to have a faith that this is the connection and all that. I wouldn't be able to make the connection if I didn't know the thing, right?

Or knowing more about the aspects or the way she acts — once you know those things, you can make that connection. So I think a lot of times when we talk about these magical things, it can be this — I don't know, for lack of a better term — like woo-woo thing. But there's this basis of learning things, like learning the facts in a sense. I feel like that's something that helped me see those things.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thanks. I think it makes sense. You're practicing both faith but also being a scholar and studying and putting that kind of karma into your mind. And by creating that karma, maybe it led to you perceiving aspects of their mandala or signs related to them. Yeah, thank you. It makes sense.

And part of it is that yeah, when a place is just a holy place of pilgrimage, it does help a little — faith and so on. But the place, the environment, the culture, et cetera, does a lot of the heavy lifting in this case. Yeah, thanks so much.

practiceReports.speaker: Dale
practiceReports.text:
I have an example of how wonderful the Lamrim practice has been on WhatsApp for me. And so, I went into the supermarket and I was waiting behind the deli counter to be served. And there were two or three people there, not looking up, not looking at me, looking very — I don't know, upset or something. And I'm just standing there waiting to be served. And I found myself getting angry — what's wrong with these people, serve me!

Okay, so finally they did, but then I went to the checkout in the same place. And everybody looked very sullen, and not happy. Not happy at all. So I left the store feeling, well, that wasn't a good experience.

But by the time I got home, I had switched that to: wait a minute, what would a bodhisattva do in this case? And I thought about it and I said, these people, who knows what's going on in their life? You need to give them compassion from my heart, and a sense of giving, a sense of giving from the heart. So I know that really affected me and changed — switched my whole attitude to that situation.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thanks, Dale. So it sounds like it was really your practice of Lamrim, and because of that — maybe it was your day, or related to when you practiced bodhichitta — and as a result of that being actively in your mind, you had this kind of difficult interaction, but then that sort of triggered this virtue coming as a response instead of just some ordinary response like self-righteousness, or just denial, or just running on with the day, busyness, or whatever. That's your point, right? It's like it was really coming from that Lamrim practice that you're putting energy into.

practiceReports.speaker: Dale
practiceReports.text: Absolutely. And I love the way it felt. I love that the way it felt in my heart — no anger. Ah, I get it, I understand. These people need just the opposite. And you can give it to them silently and in your heart. Yeah.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Thanks, Dale. Yeah, it's beautiful. And it's an interesting thing too, because you were practicing trying to live like a bodhisattva would. And one of the qualities of the Lamrim is that all the meditations up to bodhichitta are within bodhichitta. And Geshe-la explains this in various places — he says the bodhichitta is the quintessential butter that arises when the milk of Dharma is churned, that basically the mind of bodhichitta has all those other Lamrim meditations inside of it. It's just a compound mind that actually necessarily needs all of those realizations.

So by practicing Lamrim, you're seeding a bodhichitta mind the whole time. Every time you go through every single one of those previous meditations. So then kind of accessing such a profound attitude — what would a bodhisattva do? — in a situation, that actually works, because we created the karma to have a bodhichitta mind. Versus if we don't do it and you just try to do that, there's not much sort of inroads for bodhichitta in there. It's a pretty complex mind, bodhichitta — it depends on 30 or 40 different realizations that you have to put effort into. And they all are like this sort of edifice or something that the mind of bodhichitta is built on. So it just shows the value and the benefits of the Lamrim meditations. Thank you very much. Yeah.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Okay, let's look at the book. Let's see, so we're beginning a new chapter — Chapter 3, yippee! Called Full Acceptance of Bodhichitta. And basically this chapter has a couple of main parts. One is finishing up with seven limbs and merit and so on, and a bit about merit in general. Part 2 is kind of really letting in bodhichitta — to the bodhisattva vow. And then Part 3 is this slightly peculiar section called Concluding Activities, which just has some awesome little bits and nuggets and treasures in it. So that's the sort of structure of this chapter.

Okay, so Full Acceptance of Bodhichitta, page 111 in the new book. Before our mind is ready to accept and hold the precious thought of bodhichitta, it must be cleansed of its defilements and endowed with great merit. This process is similar to that by which a farmer prepares his field for a crop. First he must remove the rocks and weeds, and then he must make sure that the ground is provided with sufficient water and proper nourishment. Only then can he feel confident that the seeds he sows will sprout, grow, and ripen as he desires.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
It's interesting — just this one paragraph, right? Check: did my mind really engage with it? Like, was it really engaging with the words and the meaning? Was it going like, okay, hmm — 'before my mind is ready to accept and hold the precious thought of bodhichitta.' Ah — does it mean to be ready to accept bodhichitta? I thought you just develop bodhichitta. What do you mean, accept? Like, accept is like accept a deal, or accept something from someone else. You are letting it in. Oh, what does it mean to accept? Why would I not accept bodhichitta? If it was on offer, wouldn't I accept it? Huh. So there is a state where I am not ready to accept it in. Why would that be the case?

And 'hold' — what does that mean? Hold the precious thought? So why — to let bodhichitta in, does it involve cleansing of defilements and endowing our mind with great merit? So when we read something like that, we don't want to — we want to ask, do I live that? Do I live that truth? Not do I understand it. I mean, do I understand it is a nice question too. Does it make sense? Can I logically wrap my head around it? Why do I need merit to have bodhichitta? What is the connection between merit and bodhichitta, and cleansing of defilements and bodhichitta?

So it's not just 'do I understand it' but then, do I live it? Like, do I have it in my mental DNA — the way I live and think and operate in my life — where I am really living this idea? I need merit. I really need it. Why? Not for a nice car, or the coolest apartment, or a lot of fame or fortune or whatever. Because I want bodhichitta so badly.

I'm just belaboring the point a little bit, but I'm sort of reflecting on this from — we just studied a bit for the exam, and I had that very good opportunity to study for a few weeks on the International Teacher Training Program. And when we study Dharma, we read a little bit more closely, hopefully. And when we read closely, the Dharma comes alive. And it is filled with questions and things that stimulate our mind and make us wonder and dream and become curious and analyze and explore. It is very stimulating, actually, when we read Dharma closely.

What happens very easily is that our mind doesn't actually read the Dharma. It reads a projection. And the projection is just sort of a flattened placeholder for what is there, for the words that are there. Often the mind is just checking — if it is something that we are not that familiar with or not. And if it is something we are familiar with, what the mind actually projects is: already know this, move on. It is almost like those are the words it is seeing — already know this, move on. It's interesting, the mind does this.

I was trying to make the point a little bit in the WhatsApp group about transcribing Dharma. And I found this is a great way to start to break out of this when you're studying — I will write down a paragraph or a line or something. As we do that, we might realize, whoa, I didn't actually engage with this paragraph. My mind said it engaged with it, but it didn't. Because as I am writing it down now, I'm really trying to see some of these points as new, in a fresh way, and repealing the little shortcuts of the mind that make us not engage with it.

Maybe we can come up with some techniques of doing so — like, what are some actual practical ways to prevent us from just filling in the meaning in a way that's contrary to what's there, and that prevents us from engaging with the text in a curious and happy, inspired way? Okay, so we didn't even get into rocks and weeds and all that.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
While preparing our mind for the precious bodhichitta, there are traditional methods of purifying non-virtue and accumulating merit that should be followed. These are all contained within what is known as the practice of the seven limbs. The first three limbs have already been introduced in chapter two: prostration, offering, and confession of non-virtue.

Shantideva introduces the remaining four in this chapter: rejoicing in virtue, requesting the Buddhas to turn the Wheel of Dharma, beseeching the Buddhas not to pass away, and dedicating merit.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
We should be frothing at the mouth that we're about to look at the next four of the seven limbs, right? We should be feral. Exciting is fine. Yeah, excited is good. We'll take that. That's from excited to full-on werewolf frenzy, okay? So you've got to be somewhere in there. Yeah, Mimi's going feral.

When we're reading something like this, one of the ways to bring it alive is, again, to think — this is coming from an omniscient mind. These are Buddhist teachings, right? So Buddha is this omniscient mind that appeared in this world, and people finally realized Buddha was enlightened, and then started asking him millions of questions, because they gained access to this clairvoyant, all-knowing mind. And they sort of realized at some point, whoa, this is a mind that knows everything. So what would you do if you met a mind that knows everything? You'd start asking them millions of questions. You'd pay attention to every word. And you go, tell me about that. How do you be happy? What do you do with this situation? What if this goes wrong? Where does this come from? How should you live a good life? What about this? What about that? What happens after you die? What's a self? You just get as much as possible.

So that's what they did. That's why Buddha famously taught 84,000 teachings. So you just imagine being there when they asked Buddha originally, and he taught about the seven limbs. It'd be amazing. People were probably asking something like, how do you be happy? And he explained you need merit, and purifying negativity, and receiving blessings. And they're like, okay, cool. I've got omniscience right here. Now tell me more. How do you do that? And he's like, don't worry, there's seven things you have to do. You're like, wow, it's very specific. But that's — yeah, of course, it wouldn't be eight. It wouldn't be four. It's seven things that you do. There's like preparatory practices. That's where the teaching comes from. And then Buddha taught them.

And so when we read, if we connect to that idea — like, wow, this all-knowing mind explained these points — then they come alive in a very different way. If we think of a text as like a novel, or a self-help book, or something that has imperfections in any way, then it's very easy to just fill in our own stuff. But if we think it's coming from omniscience, a perfect mind of Buddha, then every word, every syllable becomes electric.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Each of the seven limbs serves as a direct opponent to a particular delusion, although the effect of the seven-limb practice is more far-reaching than this. Specifically, prostration destroys the delusion of pride. So we can ask — have we ever been in a state of pride and thought, I'm going to prostrate now as my solution? Like, that's what I need to do right now. I'm feeling prideful. Okay, now it's time to prostrate. And we can do an experiment like that.

While the practice of making offerings helps to overcome our miserliness. The confession of non-virtue through the application of the four opponent powers fights all three poisonous delusions of ignorance, attachment, and anger, but it's principally directed against our ignorance. That's intriguing — why is that?

Rejoicing in the virtues of others overcomes jealousy. That's quite straightforward. While requesting the Buddhas to turn the Wheel of Dharma helps to purify our wrong views and any previously committed irreligious acts. By beseeching the Buddhas not to pass away, we remove dangers and obstacles to our own life and plant seeds that eventually ripen in our attainment of the indestructible body of a Buddha. Finally, by dedicating our merit to the benefit of all sentient beings, we overcome the demon of self-cherishing.

In this chapter, Shantideva explains that the seven limbs of practice — specifically the last four — prepare us for full acceptance of bodhichitta through our formal taking of the bodhisattva vows. Thus, this chapter can be outlined as follows: How to accept and hold on to the actual bodhichitta — this is three parts. Preparatory Practices for Accumulating Merit, Fully Accepting Bodhichitta, Concluding Activities. P-A-C, that works too.

Preparatory Practices for Accumulating Merit — as indicated before, this section consists of the last four of the seven limbs with an additional explanation on training the mind in the practice of giving. Thus, this section is divided into five parts as follows: Rejoicing in virtue, Requesting the Buddhas to turn the Wheel of Dharma, Beseeching the Buddhas not to pass away, Dedicating merit, Training the mind in giving.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
I'll just do this one paragraph and then we'll take a break. Rejoicing is a joyful mind, free of jealousy and pride, which takes delight in witnessing the virtuous actions of others, or even ourself. Rejoicing in the virtue of others brings us great merit, while rejoicing in our own virtue increases our merit abundantly. It is said that rejoicing is a principal practice of a bodhisattva. Even though we may be unable to rejoice as fully as such a high-minded being, we can still practice in a similar way. It is a vast practice, extremely effective for taming the wild elephant of our mind. It is entirely appropriate to spend an entire lifetime in the practice of rejoicing.

So we might know — when we take the bodhisattva vows each day, we say: I go for refuge to the Three Jewels and confess individually our negative actions. I rejoice in the virtues of all beings and promise to accomplish a Buddha's enlightenment. So — I go for refuge to the Three Jewels: that's refuge practice, entering into refuge. And confess individually our negative actions: that's basically purifying all the negativity in our mind. And then rejoice in the virtues of all beings: it's basically saying that's sufficient to get all the merit you need. And then promise to accomplish a Buddha's enlightenment.

So as we go through this section on rejoicing, we can kind of call back to what we started the class with, which is that this is a very relaxed and easy practice. And this is a gigantic strength of it. It's very relaxed. It's very easy. Probably the biggest flaw with it is that it's so easy that you almost feel like you have to do more. Like, is that really it? Is that enough?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
And the answer is yes, it really is. If we do it kind of in a skillful way, it's enough. Why? Because you just keep getting tons of merit everywhere you go, without doing anything. You're doing nothing outwardly, and you're just getting everything that everyone else is doing. You're just — you're like a CEO. You're just doing nothing and just getting everything that everyone else gets.

You can just lay in bed. You bring your little snacks in there, and you have your blanket. Get your eye mask on, right? And you just sit there, and you just do this. Put a little smile on, because you know how much merit you're getting. You just put your little arms up like that, and you just rejoice in everyone else. And you do nothing. And you're just dripping in merit. You're just so full of spiritual realizations by the end of it all. You probably would just become a Buddha, laying there. Just chilling out.

So, yeah, anyway, we'll take a break now. But the point of this is like, it's trying to really connect this restfulness with this practice. And an understanding of emptiness with this practice, which is part of the reason why you can do it, and why it works, and why it's so restful.

announcements.speaker: Kadam Kyle
