So really time to hopefully work towards integration of our practice of Highest Yoga Tantra in a greater way. So if you're around, please do come along that day.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: Okay, so let's dedicate now. We'll come back at 6:12. We can think through the virtues we collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Apologies online people, we were eight minutes late, which is a few too many minutes. So I should have either said a later time, or we should have gone back a little earlier. So apologies if you were waiting there.

Okay, so we're continuing in rejoicing, page 113. Jealousy is the opponent of the mind of rejoicing. It generally arises towards someone more learned or fortunate than ourself. While rejoicing in others' good fortune brings us happiness and benefit, jealousy does nothing but harm our mind. If we can practice rejoicing sincerely, two beneficial results will follow. Firstly, we will plant seeds for gaining good qualities similar to the ones in which we are rejoicing. Secondly, by cultivating this mind of joy, we can overcome the poison of jealousy. It's extremely worthwhile. Jealousy not only destroys our virtue and pulls us down, but also makes it impossible for us to develop the precious bodhichitta.

Okay, so jealousy in general just means you're unhappy about someone's good fortune. Sometimes it's used interchangeably with envy and covetousness, which means more like wanting what someone else has. Sometimes in our modern speak, we use these interchangeably, but technically jealousy doesn't mean envy. We usually have both — you're not happy if someone has something good going for them, and you want it. But jealousy specifically is just simply: I'm unhappy that you're happy. It's a very simple kind of mind.

It's very useful to watch the mind and notice jealousy. It's a bit pernicious. There's really obvious gross forms, and there's little subtle bubbles of jealousy that will come up. Someone just gives us a little bit of good news, and we go, uh. Maybe we have a class that we teach at the Dharma Center, and no one goes ever, and then someone says, I taught a class and all those people went — uh. That's jealousy, right?

It's a little unhappy that they're happy. It's a sad mind. It doesn't even get you what they have. It's just turning all the happiness in the world into a cause of pain. There's not even that much happiness in the world. It's just a sad state of affairs.

The point is, it's very helpful to watch it, and notice the obvious forms — but then the more subtle forms, like in the family, little sibling competitiveness and rivalries. Or maybe a sibling's kids versus your kids. The sibling says, Johnny is going to this great university — uh. Just a little pain, a little twinge of pain. So we can sort of watch it in these kinds of situations, and we'll notice there's these little bubbles of jealousy that arise.

There's more obvious forms, which turn to malice. Which is like people in the news that we don't like. Something good happens for them — oh, I'm unhappy that they're happy. It turns into malice very quickly. Oh, I want them to suffer, actually. That's one of the ten non-virtuous actions, which is very, very bad. It's a very negative action. Many people practice this every day, when they wake up — they practice malice by zoning out in front of the news. It's just not healthy for the mind to practice malice, practice wishing harm on others. It's very negative for our spiritual development.

So, yeah, the point is obvious and clear. Let's all try to watch these little bubbles of jealousy.

teaching.speaker: Anne K
teaching.text: I hope this is not too unrelated, but that little feeling of pleasure when misfortune strikes someone — I think it's kind of related. And it's like, what's the opponent to that?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, it's malice light. Malice light. Yeah, basically, because there's actually — what's it called — wrong rejoicing, I think is the technical name. But you're basically rejoicing in someone's misfortune. It's very related to malice. But it's definitely a non-virtuous action, for sure.

Rejoicing in the misfortune of others — again, very common activity, right? It's like, let's all get around the water cooler, let's celebrate some misfortune that's befalling someone. Mass media, not helpful for this kind of thing. Yeah, a little delight when bad things happen to people. It's so easy, actually, because sometimes we can justify it — like, that's going to help them grow. Yeah, they brought it on themselves, and fair is fair. Karma — it's just karma, ha ha ha. So devious, kind of nasty minds. Anyway, we're all going to work on that.

teaching.speaker: Jose
teaching.text: So based on what you just said — so if I'm watching the news from a specific side, and they are reporting about the other side regarding politics, and they take a stand and an opinion, and they're showing the — what's the right word in English — the hilarious side of the other people protesting, like if it's phony or not, like how phony it is or whatever. And I'm watching, and yeah, they're right. It is phony or whatever. So you're saying this is negative action, negative karma?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah. We're not trying to be lawyers here, right?

teaching.speaker: Jose
teaching.text: Because if that's the case, I have to stop completely watching news.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
No, we're trying not to be rulesy here, okay? And we're not trying to create some kind of rigid rule. Because Dharma is about watching our mind, right? It's not about these sort of rigid stances about what to do externally or not to do externally.

So let's not try to create some rule or decree, but in those situations, it's just very helpful to do what you asked Mimi earlier — and you pressed her: what's your intention right now? And then you check a little further. What's your intention, really? What's really the intention? And then that will naturally create an answer about what to do. So that's what you should do. And if you notice the intention is something non-virtuous, then yeah, stop, don't do it. If the intention is whatever — maybe something neutral or positive — then it could be fine.

There's nothing wrong with satire, or laughing at something ludicrous, or laughing at the delusions. That can even be a very positive action. Wow, look at that, those are crazy delusions, ha ha ha. But if we're then wishing misfortune on people or criticizing people or judging people, then yeah, it's ventured into a non-virtuous action.

So you've got to just look at your own mind, I think. I've generally found that most of my attitudes around anything political are pretty much deluded, generally speaking. So it's just very hard to not have a kind of very base mindset with a lot of these things, because they're very tribal. And a lot of the way that it's talked about is portrayed in a very tribal way. It's designed to incite that part of us that's tribal, not rational and human. And this is very effective.

So of course you can have an opinion. I want less taxes, I want more taxes, I want more services, I want not to spend so much money on these services. I want to go to war, I don't want to go to war. I want this candidate, I want that candidate. You can have all those opinions in a completely balanced way. It's like saying, I'd like the carpet in here to be a different color or something. It can be completely balanced. It's just for a lot of us and what we actually interact with, it becomes tribal and base. And in those cases, we have to watch our mind and think: is that what we really want to be doing with our time?

I often find it very helpful just to think like Buddha and I are doing things together. I've had some good fortune to spend kind of one-on-one time hosting a very precious teacher to me in different places that I've been — taking them around the town, and maybe they live in the same apartment for a little bit. And what I've noticed is that my behavior, when I'm with them, is very nice and virtuous. And I don't do any distracting, stupid things. And my mind is just very happy and peaceful and contented and not wandering towards nonsense.

Well, why is that? The Buddhas are around us all the time. So why is it that having this person who I really admire — all of a sudden the behavior changes? Ah, that's a sign I'm not feeling in the presence of the Buddhas.

So if I was in the presence of that teacher, who I deeply admire and I really look up to, would I say, hey so-and-so, I've got these little videos where this really great comedian's making a fool of people and showing how stupid they are — do you want to watch it with me? We can laugh how stupid they are together. You can even imagine doing it together with them. And just — would you do that? Yeah, probably not.

So it's like, huh — Buddhas are with us all the time, they're at our heart all the time. And so what do we want to do with them all day?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Okay, so I'm not trying to make a rule. It's just about looking at our own mind.

When we rejoice in the happiness and comfort of others, we create the cause for enjoying such experiences ourself. However, if the comfort of others provokes jealousy in our mind, we will experience unhappiness in both the present and future. How wonderful it would be if this poisonous mind could be eliminated forever. It has not a single positive aspect, but instead is responsible for many of the disputes and conflicts plaguing the world today. From fights between neighbors to wars between nations, a frequent source of conflict is the deluded mind of jealousy.

Generally speaking, if we don't like someone, we probably have some kind of jealousy towards them too — we're unhappy when they're happy. So anyone we don't like, there's probably some sort of tainted mind there, some kind of jealousy and other things like anger.

I think this is really clear, and I think our Sangha is just a very beautiful and inspiring example. But jealousy in a Sangha is like an insoluble, cancerous thing — it's like a kidney stone or something, just something very solid and destructive and painful. So I think our Sangha is very beautiful and harmonious, but it's just a reminder.

The little group in England is very beautiful, and many people acted in a way that demonstrated they were exchanging self with others. Multiple times, over and over again, in exemplary ways. And then in general, that happens a lot here — there's so much care and compassion. So I'm not saying this in a pointed way. I'm just saying it as a cautionary tale.

What I've seen in centers where a jealous mind takes root is that what happens is it spreads until there's two factions. And usually what happens is the jealous faction prevents the other faction from continuing. They just all leave. But then all you have is the jealous faction, and then they eat each other alive until there's nothing. And then, and only then, it gets to restart again. It's like a boil that got popped. Any group is like that. I haven't seen it in a while, but I have seen it with my eyes, and it's a very sad kind of thing.

So I just wanted to make that point. Sometimes it's like, this is something we've got to really work on. I don't think it is particularly in our Sangha — I think it's very beautiful and supportive. But it's just good to know, in case you notice it happen. At some point go — ooh, this isn't one of those delusions that I can be patient with. It's a delusion I have to be kind of vicious with and intolerant of. Make sense?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
How can jealousy be uprooted? As with all delusions, the ultimate solution is to understand that the root of jealousy is our self-grasping ignorance. Only the direct realization of emptiness, the direct realization that all things lack inherent existence, can cut through the root of this ignorance. However, before we are in a position to apply this ultimate solution, we can and should use the temporary antidotes presented in Dharma teachings. Thus, in the same way that our anger is lessened by our practice of love and patience, and our attachment can be lessened by meditating upon desirable objects' unpleasant and repulsive characteristics, so too can we counteract the jealous mind by rejoicing in the virtues of others. By weakening and then utterly uprooting our delusions in this way, we can eventually gain complete liberation from all suffering.

So this is about applying opponents. Rejoicing is the opponent to jealousy. This is just one of those kindnesses of Buddha — to explain the opponents. I didn't know about them until I studied Buddhism. And many people still don't know about them. They don't know that there's an opponent.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
One who has gained such freedom from him or herself is called an arhat or foe destroyer. Yet after eradicating all the delusions, the imprints of the delusions still remain. These imprints are called obstructions to knowing, or obstructions to omniscience, because they prevent the mind from gaining an uninterrupted perception of the true nature of all phenomena. Through developing bodhichitta and practicing Mahayana teachings, even these subtle obstructions to omniscience can be removed. One who has not only eradicated all his or her delusions but removed the shroud of their imprints as well has become a fully enlightened being, a Buddha.

Abandoning delusions is like removing musk from a box, and purifying the imprints preventing enlightenment is like removing the odor that remains behind. Also, Geshe-la does garlic and the smell of garlic, which we're probably more familiar with that.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
The path leading to the attainment of enlightenment is a steady development of our positive qualities of mind. Each step of spiritual training brings us closer to the goal. Of all those practices on the path, the simplest and most effective is to rejoice in virtue. As the great Tibetan meditator Guntang Jampalyong said: if you wish to accumulate a great deal of merit, even while lying down, then rejoice in the virtue of others.

Yes. So no guilt when we've got to lie down, right? No sort of Protestant work ethic stuff coming up in that moment. I've got to be more productive, right? I've got to do more in my life.

Being outwardly productive has nothing to do with a better world, right? Is there any link between a better world and people being outwardly productive? Is there a causal link? No. The world is worse in a lot of ways because of people's productivity and their incredible work ethic.

So it's like, you never have to feel guilty or whatever we feel if we're not doing some external activity. We can put all that down. What matters is what we're doing with our mind. It really doesn't matter what we're doing externally. It's what we're doing with our mind that matters. Then if on the basis of doing something negative with our mind, we do something negative externally — yeah, then that's a negative action. But that's really because of the mind.

So it would be nice as we kind of go through this chapter just to look at this a bit. Do we have this kind of guilt around lack of productivity? Do we sort of associate virtue and outer productivity? Do we kind of view that as a virtuous thing? Like, we view someone who's not as active outwardly as less virtuous than someone who's really active and industrious?

Like, you're sick, really sick — do you have some reticence against calling out of work, which you're totally allowed to do? This is actually good for the other people for you not to get them sick. But do you have a feeling like, no, the courageous and strong thing to do is to bust in there and make everyone sick and be miserable all day?

If we notice that in us, then we might notice that it gets into our Dharma practice in some ways too — this sort of desire for something performative, or kind of doing things that are external as a reason to not do something that's internal.

So the summary of all this is that ultimately, all that matters is what we're doing with our mind. That's all that matters. It's not what we're doing externally. And so we don't need to be rushing around and doing so much and whatever. What we want to be hyper-vigilant about is what we're doing with our mind, what we're thinking about all day. That's what we want to be vigilant about.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
When King Prasenajit asked Buddha Shakyamuni for a spiritual practice he could follow without having to abandon his family or kingdom, Buddha advised him to practice rejoicing, cultivate bodhichitta, and dedicate his merits. Even someone who's very busy with the affairs of the world has time to engage in these three practices, and a great deal of positive energy can be generated by each of them.

The ability to rejoice wholeheartedly in the virtuous actions of ourself and others is based on our appreciation of the positive effects of these actions. The more we understand that happiness will be the result of a particular practice, the more we'll be able to rejoice in it. In his Guide, Shantideva mentions three areas of activity worthy of rejoicing: activities involved in achieving a higher state of birth either as a god or human, complete liberation from suffering, and the fully enlightened state of a Buddha. This is related to the three scopes — it's basically rejoicing in activities that lead to the three scopes. What are those? It's basically Lamrim. That's what leads to the three scopes. Attaining the happiness of the three scopes.

The first — all the virtuous activity achieving happiness in future states of existence — is often called the temporary result of spiritual practice. The ultimate result of spiritual practice is known as definite goodness, and comprises the attainment of personal liberation for the practitioner mainly concerned with his or her own welfare, and full enlightenment for the practitioner mainly concerned with the welfare of others. These three states of attainment are characterized by increasing levels of happiness and peace, and are therefore worthy of rejoicing.

Shantideva begins his section by rejoicing in the virtuous causes and effects of fortunate states of existence. The causes for being born in one of these states as either a human or a god include the practices of moral discipline, giving, and stainless prayer. By engaging in selfless giving, keeping our moral discipline pure, practicing patience, making the appropriate prayers, and so forth, we can avoid the three lower realms and gain a higher rebirth. In addition, if we rejoice in others who are also following these pure practices, this would be the cause of even more benefit and merit for ourself.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
The story is told of the king mentioned before, Prasenajit, who invited the Buddha and his entire retinue to his palace for a grand feast. Standing at the door was a beggar who rejoiced in the king's generosity but was saddened to think that he did not have the opportunity to perform such virtuous actions because he himself was poor. At the end of the banquet, Buddha, who understood the minds of all who were present, dedicated the merits of the beggar and not those of the patron of the meal, as was customary.

It's funny that this is the same person — the king who gave the advice to, or that Buddha gave the advice to about learning to rejoice. The king, with great surprise, asked Buddha why he had done this. Buddha replied: on this occasion, the beggar has practiced purer virtue than you. The virtue of your offerings has been stained with worldly thoughts of reputation, pride, and the like, whereas the virtue of the beggar's rejoicing was unmixed with such impurities. Thus I have dedicated his merits.

It's very useful to have an omniscient being around, because then you can just take what they have to say. You can't argue with it, and you know their meaning. They're only coming from the best place. So you're like, touché. Fair enough, Buddha. You're right.

So this is a great story to ponder. There's a sort of big outer show versus the person who's just doing this simple positive action, kind of very humbly. And the big outer show — it's not particularly clear that it was even positive. But the beggar's rejoicing was very, very pure. So again, it's an invitation to use rejoicing in our life, because generally speaking, it's a very, very positive action — very pure and unstained.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Next, Shantideva rejoices in the teachings that lead all sentient beings from their pain and suffering in samsara to the rest and peace of liberation. There are many paths that lead to the attainment of liberation, but they're all included in the three higher trainings of moral discipline, concentration, and wisdom. Ordinary moral discipline — abandonment of the ten non-virtuous actions — can lead to rebirth as a human or god, but is not adequate by itself for the attainment of liberation. For this, the moral discipline of renunciation for the whole of samsara is required. When moral discipline is conjoined with the thought of renunciation, it earns the title 'higher moral discipline.' In a similar fashion, with renunciation as their base, the practices of single-pointed concentration and insight into the true nature of reality become the trainings in higher concentration and higher wisdom. When these three higher trainings are completed, the practitioner will definitely attain liberation.

Okay, so we'll do some more on that next class.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
But I just want to read a little bit from Great Treasury of Merit about rejoicing. So in general, we say rejoicing is a very pure action, but there's something that makes it completely pure, which is remembering emptiness.

So Geshe-la says here, page 193, Great Treasury of Merit: In the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, Buddha teaches that bodhisattvas on the path of meditation should practice rejoicing while remembering the emptiness of all phenomena. Rejoicing is completely pure when it is free from grasping at inherent existence. Otherwise, it remains a contaminated virtue.

So it will still lead to good results, but it will just lead to good samsaric results.

According to the words of the sadhana, we rejoice in the dreamlike happiness and pure white virtue of others. Learning to see all phenomena as like a dream is the best way of overcoming grasping at their inherent existence. In a dream, phenomena appear to be real, existing from their own side, but in reality, they're merely projected by the mind. Even though dream objects are merely imputed by mind, they exist in function. As Chandrakirti points out in Guide to the Middle Way, a man can dream of an attractive woman during the night, and when he wakes up the next day, continue to feel attachment toward her. Thus, even though the dream woman is merely an imputation of mind, she can function to generate attachment. In the same way, all the phenomena of our waking life — our environment, bodies, minds, and enjoyments — are merely imputed by mind, but they exist nevertheless and function in many different ways. If we view the happiness and virtues of others in this way, when we practice rejoicing, our action will be completely virtuous and produce very powerful results.

And just to remind us of the verse, it's just one of those lovely verses that we do in the sadhana: Though phenomena have no sign of inherent existence, from the depths of our heart we rejoice in all the dreamlike happiness and pure white virtue that arise for ordinary and superior beings.

So there's a few things here. One is just, we can do this with every practice. We just try to remember emptiness in some way, and it doesn't have to be a very conceptual thing. You're just remembering it loosely — going, okay, I'm generating love for this dreamlike person. Or I'm practicing patience with this dreamlike difficult person. Or I'm doing meditation right now in a dream. I'm doing a dream meditation in a dream world. It doesn't have to be a huge analysis.

But the point is trying to remember it while practicing something else, some other virtue. And we'll notice it will really, really improve it — it'll make it much more effective and precise. And we'll notice with certain practices where the effects aren't as obvious — like ones that are just about creating good karma — bringing in this idea that everything is like a dream while you do it makes it actually make sense. Where if everything was sort of out there and independent of the mind, it just doesn't make that much sense. Like, how does making offerings make your life better if everything is inherent? It just doesn't really make sense. But if everything is like a dream, we'll start to see how offerings make perfect sense.

With rejoicing in particular, the idea is dreamlike happiness that we're rejoicing in. They're not a real person experiencing happiness. They're a dreamlike person experiencing dreamlike happiness.

Okay, so as we practice the bodhisattva's way of life, we want to do this more and more. We want to bring in just a simple understanding of emptiness whenever we engage in these method practices. In Ocean of Nectar, for example, with every perfection, Geshe-la does this — explains the perfection in general, but then explains how it becomes a pure practice. And it's by remembering emptiness in some way.

Basically what it explains is that virtue, when we don't remember emptiness, is like food laced with poison. This comes from Buddha. Why? Because we're creating just happiness and some sorrow. Which again, is way better than unhappiness and some sorrow. But if you're going to do the virtue anyway, you might as well just add a little bit more to make it a dreamlike happiness and joy and deep peace and liberation.

So please play around with this a little bit with all your virtues. But as maybe we practice rejoicing in this week ahead, just see what's the difference in thinking: I'm rejoicing in their dreamlike happiness, as opposed to I'm rejoicing in their real happiness. Just see the difference in the feeling of that.

teaching.speaker: Adriana
teaching.text:
Kadam Kyle, I have a question about remaining natural while changing your intention. And if you have any go-to tips, tricks for when — because I think this kind of rejoicing in negativity is a really prevalent activity in samsara. So I know I struggle with like, oh, but like saying something like, but you know, they're suffering or something. And then people are like, you're annoying, you know, who are you?

And I'm thinking about my mom, where she could talk for an hour about how awful everyone is. And I've been practicing patience, so I'm listening, but I'm trying not to agree at the same time. And so I sometimes try to imagine — what will she be like when this is all purified? But it's hard to do it in the moment. So I wonder if you have any advice.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, I totally get your point here. So when we're in ordinary conversations and there's somewhat non-virtuous speech occurring, or just ordinary speech — how do we operate? Because we don't want to necessarily be increasing our non-virtues. We also don't want to be offending and bothering the people we're with by being pious or holier than them or whatever, or just seeming kind of weird. And then creating negativity.

So yeah, maybe one thing to start is that we need a very certain stance in general. And the certain stance in general is that we're far more interested in what's happening in our own mind than what's happening in the conversation. We're just so much more interested and intrigued about the inner world than whatever's happening externally. Doesn't mean that we're callous and we're not paying attention. But like 80%, 90% of our mind is actually intrigued — what am I thinking about right now?

And that stance really helps with these kind of situations, because we start to shift the weight of what's most important in the conversation. The way the ordinary world works is that the outer situation is like 100% of what's important. What's going on in people's inner state is literally 0% important. And then we start practicing Dharma — we might move to 80-20. The outer situation is like 80% of what's important, and the inner is like 20%. But the real rate is inverted, basically. The inner situation is infinitely more important than the words being said in the conversation.

I always remember Geshe-la's statement, which is very close to when he died, and he said: this is not my environment. Talking about the outer world — this is not my environment. And the more we start to practice, for example, Highest Yoga Tantra, we start to feel the ordinary appearances of life — they're not our environment. They're not the real world. They're not our environment. And so a big portion of our mental energy is put being in the real world. And then we sort of feel that the person floating around talking to people is just like a little avatar or something that we're controlling. But it's not the real world — it's just this ordinary appearance that hasn't been purified yet.

And so in those cases, if our mind is right, then our job verbally — unless someone is very open to our guidance and help — is pretty much just to make them happy in whatever way we can. Because if they're not open to our help, there's not much that we can say otherwise. And so then we're just trying to remain natural completely. If we're very invested in the outer situation, then these kind of situations become incredibly complex and complicated, because we're trying to control it in just the right way. And it's almost impossible to find the right outer solution in these situations.

And of course, with skill, we do improve over time. We learn how to change the conversation, how to say the right thing, how to help people look on the bright side. But most of that skill comes from prioritizing the inner world. And then on the outside, basically just helping people stay happy in whatever way we can.

For me, I just think of it as a few buckets for people. Bucket one is basically non-negotiable commitment people in my life that I just have to keep in my life — parents, siblings, certain Sangha friends and so on. They're just like — I'm committed, I'm in it for the long haul until I die. I'm going to do my best. It's like bucket one, non-negotiable people.

And then bucket two is people that I've chosen to be around and spend time with, but it's completely negotiable as long as it stays virtuous. And right now it's virtuous and positive and helpful for both parties — like Sangha friends. So yeah, it's good for them, it's good for me. Let's keep it going.

And bucket three is basically no thanks, I've got better things to do. Oh sorry, and bucket four is just strangers — random strangers.

So bucket three, the no-thanks group, is like people where I was trying to sort of control the relationship in some way to make it positive or virtuous. They have no interest. I can't do anything about it. No thanks, moving on. And it's very easy to have a kind of martyrdom, a martyr mind, to try to maintain those relationships and hold on to them — forgetting that we're abandoning every other living being while doing that, in the name of this one relationship that we're trying to hold on to. And usually when we do that, it's because of our pride. We don't want to let go and realize it's just not going anywhere. And it's actually much kinder for both parties to let go.

I'm just sharing this with respect to this point, Adriana, because with your mom — that's a bucket one person, a commitment person. So yeah, we have to figure out how to be with that person in a way that makes sense — probably just making them happy while just training our mind the whole time. And if it's long conversations that don't seem to make tons of sense, what I might do in that situation is dump 95% of my mental energy into my mental world and 5% into the conversation. And then it's very happy — I'm just in a meditation with them. My eyes are open and the mind is somewhere else. It's very peaceful and happy, nodding along.

Anyway, she's a bucket one. But sometimes there's people in that third bucket, where we're trying to make it something virtuous when it's just not going to be particularly. And in those cases, it's just better to move on, not in a callous way, but for that person and all living beings.

So those are the two points I wanted to make. One is: what percentage of my energy is being put in my mind and what percentage is sort of on the outside? And then trying to see — who are these people? Okay, can I make them happy? That's my main job. And then inwardly, I'm just doing something virtuous while I'm doing my best to make them happy. And then over time, yeah, we'll get skill, techniques and so on that will come, without trying to force it.

Yeah, good point about bringing this into our Lamrim practice. Exactly, because it goes perfectly. Admiring faith is the same kind of nature as rejoicing. Rejoicing is in the nature of admiring faith. And admiring faith makes every Lamrim object work.

So even before you do any Lamrim object, you can just rejoice in it. Rejoice in the realization of death. Rejoice in the realization of Precious Human Life. Rejoice in the realization of the dangers of lower rebirth. Rejoice in what it would be like for you to have it one day. Rejoice in everyone who has that experience. Yeah, so it's a great idea to kind of blend it with our Lamrim practice. And then our TTP practice is not siloed and separate from our own Lamrim practice that we do. They're just mutually supportive — they're like one thing. Thank you.
